Assignment 2. Naming 3. Functions 4. Vectors ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/map.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: # Assignment ::: {.section-art} {{< lif "../../icons/contacts.json" state=in-reveal colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ## Assignment {.fs80} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - It helps to store data in [named objects]{.b .green} - This makes the data easier to use and re-use - And the code easier to write and read ::: {.fragment .mt1} - Which command is easier to follow? 1. Dial *7 8 5 8 6 4 0 8 4 1* 2. Call *Office Phone* ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - Named objects come from [assignment]{.b .blue} - Give a **name** then an **arrow** then the **data** ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"} ::: {.fragment} ::: {.syntax} [Form]{.lbl} `name <- value` [Example]{.lbl} `office <- 7858640841` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Assigning and Printing ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Store the value 2 under the name x x <- 2 # Typing the name on its own prints the value x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} `<-` stores a value under a name. Assigning prints nothing; typing the name on its own is how you ask R to show you what it holds. ::: ## Using an Object in Math ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Once x exists, it stands in for its value x * 4 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # It can appear as many times as you like in one line (10 + x - 1) / x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5.5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} Wherever a value could go, a name holding that value can go instead, as often as you need it. ::: ## Updating Requires Assignment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Using x does not change it x + 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # x is still 2 x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # To update it, assign the result back to the name x <- x + 1 x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} Using an object never changes it. To update one, assign the result **back to the same name**. ::: ## Objects Can Create Other Objects ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # The right-hand side can use objects that already exist y <- 10 + x y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 13 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # And a line can use several objects at once y / x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.333333 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} The right-hand side of `<-` is just an expression, so it can use any objects that already exist. That is how a script builds up from one line to the next. ::: # Naming ::: {.section-art} {{< lif "../../icons/business_card.json" state=in-reveal colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ## Naming {.fs80} - Object names can [only include]{.b .blue}: - Letters: `a-Z` - Numbers: `0-9` - Underscores: `_` - Periods: `.` ::: {.fragment .mt1} - Additional Rules: - Must [start with a letter]{.b .blue} (or a period) - Cannot contain spaces or dashes - Cannot contain other symbols - Names are case-sensitive (`age` ≠ `Age`) ::: ## Good Names are a Balancing Act ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 93 # legal, but what is it? rate <- 93 # too short to be clear heart_rate_in_beats_per_minute <- 93 # too long to type heart_rate_bpm <- 93 # just right ``` ::: ::: {.takeaway} A good name is the shortest one a reader can still understand six months later. ::: ## Pitfall: No Spaces or Dashes ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="false"} heart rate <- 93 ``` ::: ::: {.r-error} ``` Error: unexpected symbol in "heart rate" ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="false"} heart-rate <- 93 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error: ! object 'heart' not found ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} A space stops R mid-line. A dash is worse: R reads `heart-rate` as *heart minus rate*, so it fails looking for an object rather than telling you the name is illegal. Use an underscore: `heart_rate`. ::: ## Pitfall: No Special Symbols ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="false"} age@time2 <- 12 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error: ! object 'age' not found ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} age_time2 <- 12 # correct age_time2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 12 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} `@` already means something else in R, so it reads `age@time2` as an operation on an object called `age`. Letters, numbers, `_` and `.` are all a name may hold. ::: ## Pitfall: Names Must Start with a Letter ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="false"} 1_heart_rate <- 93 ``` ::: ::: {.r-error} ``` Error: unexpected input in "1_" ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="false"} _heart_rate <- 93 ``` ::: ::: {.r-error} ``` Error: unexpected symbol in "_heart_rate" ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} heart_rate_1 <- 93 # correct: the digit comes last heart_rate_1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 93 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} Move the digit to the end and the name is fine. ::: ## Names are Case-Sensitive ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} heart_rate <- 93 Heart_rate <- 88 # These are two entirely different objects heart_rate ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 93 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} Heart_rate ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 88 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} One capital letter makes an entirely different object. R will not warn you, because it has no way to know you meant the other one. ::: # Functions ::: {.section-art} {{< lif "../../icons/gears.json" state=in-reveal colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ## Functions {.fs80} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - [Recipes]{.b .green} allow chefs to cook up tasty treats - Recipes call for ingredients - Recipes involve one or more steps - Steps transform ingredients into treats ::: {.fragment .mt1} - [Functions]{.b .blue} are like *customizable* recipes - Functions call for inputs ("arguments") - Functions involve one or more lines - Code transforms inputs into outputs - Functions usually need parentheses ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"} ::: {.fragment} ::: {.syntax} [Form]{.lbl} `output <- fn(input)` [Example]{.lbl} `out <- f(in1, in2)` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Functions Do a Task More Readably ::: {.f5} `output <- function_name(input)` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # The hard way 9 ^ (1 / 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # The readable way x <- sqrt(9) x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} A function gives a name to something you would otherwise have to spell out. It is easier to write, and far easier to read back. ::: ## What Can Go Inside a Function ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- 9 # The input can be an object rather than a literal value sqrt(y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Or the result of a calculation round(2 / 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} Anything that produces a value can go in the input slot: a literal, an object, or another calculation. R works out the inside first, then hands the result over. ::: ## Arguments Customize a Function ::: {.f5} `output <- function_name(argument, argument_name = argument_value)` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(2 / 3, digits = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.67 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # digits has a default of 0, so this... round(2 / 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # ...means exactly the same thing as this round(2 / 3, digits = 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} Extra arguments change *how* a function does its job. Most have a default, which is what you get when you leave them out. ::: # Vectors ::: {.section-art} {{< lif "../../icons/stack_list.json" state=in-reveal colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ## Vectors {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - [Vectors]{.b .blue} combine similar objects into a collection - *I like to imagine a train pulling multiple cars*
![](../../img/traincar.png) - A vector is one object with many sub-objects - We refer to each sub-object as an [element]{.b .green} ::: {.fragment .mt1} - Some functions [transform each element]{.b .green} in turn - *Double the amount of cargo in every train car* ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - Some functions [summarize across elements]{.b .green} - *Calculate the total cargo across all train cars* ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"} ::: {.fragment} ::: {.syntax} [Form]{.lbl} `name <- c(value, value)` [Example]{.lbl} `v <- c(1, 2, 3)` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Combining Elements into a Vector ::: {.f5} `vector_name <- c(element1, element2, element3)` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="false"} x <- 4 9 16 25 ``` ::: ::: {.r-error} ``` Error: unexpected numeric constant in "x <- 4 9" ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(4, 9, 16, 25) x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 9 16 25 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} y <- c(2, 3) y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} Elements must be separated by commas and wrapped in `c()`. Without it R sees several values where it expected one. ::: ## Combining Vectors and Elements ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # c() also joins whole vectors together c(x, y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 9 16 25 2 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # And vectors and single elements c(x, y, 20) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 9 16 25 2 3 20 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} `c()` flattens whatever you give it into one vector, so there is no such thing as a vector nested inside another. ::: ## Math Transforms Each Element ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x + 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 10 17 26 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x * 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 12 27 48 75 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # But as before, nothing is saved without assignment x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 9 16 25 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} An operation applies to **every element at once**, with no loop to write. As with a single value, the result is not saved unless you assign it. ::: ## Functions That Transform ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sqrt(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 3 4 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} log(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.386294 2.197225 2.772589 3.218876 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} These return a vector as long as the input: one answer per element. ::: ## Functions That Summarize ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} length(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sum(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 54 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 13.5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} average(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `average()`: ! could not find function "average" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} These collapse the whole vector to a single number. Note the last one: R names this function `mean()`, and a reasonable guess is still an error. ::: ## Pitfall: Missing Values are Contagious ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scores <- c(10, 12, 20, NA, 8) # NA spreads: the mean depends on the value we do not have mean(scores) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Ask for the mean of the non-missing values instead mean(scores, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 12.5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.takeaway} `NA` means "we do not know", so any answer depending on it is also unknown. That is a feature, not a bug. `na.rm = TRUE` answers from what you have. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
